Sermon on the Mount
SUR-muhn on thuh MOWNT
noun phrase
The Lord Jesus' great discourse in Matthew 5-7, delivered on a mountain in Galilee to His disciples in the hearing of the multitudes; the fullest single statement of the ethics of His kingdom.

See also: Sermon on the Mount · Sermon on the Mount

📖 Biblical Definition

The Sermon on the Mount is the Lord Jesus' great discourse in Matthew 5 through 7, the fullest single declaration of the character and conduct of the citizens of His kingdom. It opens with the Beatitudes, pronouncing blessing on the poor in spirit, the mourners, the meek, and the persecuted — a portrait of grace-wrought character, not a ladder of merit. The Lord then declares His relation to the law: 'Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil' (Matt 5:17), and in six antitheses drives the commandments beneath the surface to the heart — anger as murder's root, lust as adultery's seed — demanding a righteousness exceeding that of the scribes. He teaches secret giving, the Lord's Prayer, treasure in heaven, trust over anxiety, the narrow gate, and the test of fruits, and He closes with the two builders: 'whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them' builds on rock (Matt 7:24). The crowds were astonished, 'for he taught them as one having authority' (Matt 7:29). The sermon is neither a plan of salvation by works nor a beautiful impossibility: it is the law of the King for a people already His by grace, describing the life that flows from the new heart His Spirit gives.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Christ's discourse in Matthew 5-7: the Beatitudes, the law fulfilled and driven to the heart, the Lord's Prayer, treasure and trust, the narrow way, and the two builders — the ethics of the kingdom for a people saved by grace.

SERMON ON THE MOUNT, noun phrase. The Lord's discourse in Matthew 5-7.

Opens with the Beatitudes: the portrait of grace-wrought kingdom character.

Declares the law fulfilled, not destroyed, and drives it to the heart (Matt 5:17-48).

Teaches secret piety, the Lord's Prayer, treasure in heaven, and trust over anxiety.

Closes with the narrow gate, the test of fruits, and the house built on the rock.

📖 Key Scripture

Matt 5:3 — "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."

Matt 5:17 — "Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil."

Matt 7:24 — "Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock:"

Matt 7:29 — "For he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Sermon is corrupted when it is cut loose from the cross and made a self-saving ethic or a merely social program, and equally when it is postponed to another age so that its commands no longer bind the church today.

expand to see more

Ethics-without-atonement misreading. Liberal religion has long treated the Sermon as the 'real' Christianity — a noble ethic that needs no atoning blood — as though men could climb the Beatitudes to heaven. The Sermon itself forbids this: it demands a righteousness exceeding the scribes', purity of heart, perfection as the Father is perfect — a standard that slays self-righteousness and drives the sinner to the Savior who fulfilled all righteousness and bled for those who had none. The dictionary holds that the Sermon describes the fruit of salvation, never its price; severed from the cross it is not good news but a death sentence.

Postponement misreading. The opposite error defers the Sermon to a future dispensation, as though its commands were not for the church now. But the Lord closed it by binding ALL hearers to do these sayings on pain of ruin (Matt 7:24-27), and commissioned His church to teach the nations 'to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you.' The dictionary holds the Sermon as the present law of the King for His present people — kingdom ethics in force wherever the King reigns, until He comes.
